title: These Homes Are Holes in the Ground. On Purpose.
question: Why do people live in Matmata?
message: This video tells curious adults that Amazigh families in southern Tunisia built homes around deep pits in the ground because the earth keeps them cool in summer, warm in winter and hidden from view, and that a few families still choose to live that way.
angle: People live in Matmata because Amazigh families learned to dig homes around open pits in soft rock that stay cool in summer, sheltered in winter and easy to defend, and some still stay because the homes are their tradition and tourism helps keep them, despite floods that collapsed many homes, a government push to move to new towns and water that once came by camel.

scenes.narration: This is a piece of the wall beside my bed. It fell onto my pillow on my first night, like a hint. The town is Matmata. For centuries, Amazigh families, often called Berbers, have lived here in homes dug down into the earth. Not caves in a cliff. Pits, open to the sky. I wanted to know who digs a house instead of building one, and whether I could call a hole home.

scenes.role: chương 1: hành trình từ Tunis 365 km về phía nam, cảnh quan rỗ hố
scenes.narration: I started in Tunis, the capital, on the coast. Matmata is about three hundred and sixty-five kilometres to the south. That's around two hundred and twenty-five miles. I drew the route in my notebook as the land outside changed. I had booked a room underground, and I had pictured a basement with a lift and a vending machine. The landscape had other plans, and it was not ready to tell me yet. Green fields became olive groves. Olive groves became dry hills. Then palm trees in the valleys, and the ground started to look like it had been hit by a lot of very small meteors. Round dents everywhere. I thought it was erosion. The landscape seemed to be in on a joke. I did not understand the joke yet. I would understand it about an hour later, from the bottom of one of the dents. Along the way we passed a sign for the new town, with its ordinary roofs and ordinary windows. Another sign pointed past it, toward the dents, and said old Matmata. I looked where it pointed. I saw no town at all. I checked the sign again. The sign was very sure of itself.

scenes.narration: I got out of the car and looked around for the village. There were no rooftops. No walls. No windows. A few modern buildings in the distance, and otherwise just dry hills with holes in them. My guess: everybody left. A ghost town, with very tidy holes. Then I heard a goat. The goat was below me. I walked to the edge of the nearest pit and looked down. I found a courtyard, swept clean, with doorways carved into the walls. There was washing on a line, and a woman sorting olives. The village had not left. The village was downstairs.

scenes.role: mô tả cấu trúc: hố 5–10 m, sâu ≤9 m, hai tầng phòng, đường hầm vào; khoảng 365 km
scenes.narration: Here is how one of these homes works, as I learned it with my own legs. First you dig a big round pit, roughly five to ten metres across and up to about nine metres deep. That pit becomes your courtyard, your light, your air and your living room. Around its walls you carve rooms into the soft rock, often on two levels. Bedrooms, the kitchen and animal stalls go on the lower level. Storage goes up top. To get in from outside, you walk down a sloping tunnel dug through the ground. Picture a house turned inside out. Instead of windows looking out at the world, every door looks in at the family.

scenes.role: chương 3: một ngày trong nhà hố theo giờ; mát giữa trưa; Wob đổi ý lần 1
scenes.narration: I spent a full day in a pit house that now takes in guests. Early morning: the courtyard was cool and blue, and the sky was a perfect circle above me. I felt like a goldfish looking up out of its bowl. Mid-morning: the sun climbed, and the courtyard filled with light like water filling a bucket. Noon: outside, the hills were baking. I went into my room, carved into the wall, and it was noticeably cooler. One study of these homes found the inside can be up to about fifteen degrees Celsius cooler than outside in summer. That's around twenty-seven degrees Fahrenheit. I lay on the bed and listened to absolutely nothing. No traffic. No wind. Just rock, being calm. I changed my mind about holes.

scenes.role: chương 4: ba lý do: khí hậu (lớp đất cách nhiệt), đất mềm, phòng thủ; mức C về nguồn gốc
scenes.narration: So why dig down instead of building up? I asked myself this while lying very still in my cool room, which felt like cheating. There are a few reasons, and they work together. First, climate. Reuters describes these homes as having an earthen casing that protects against searing summer heat and winter winds. Picture a wine cellar. Deep enough underground, the temperature barely changes between day and night, or summer and winter. Here, the whole house is the cellar. Second, the ground itself. The rock here is soft enough to dig with simple tools. Third, safety. From a distance, these homes are almost invisible, and the only way in is a narrow sloping tunnel, easy to watch. Nobody knows for certain when or why the first pits were dug, and accounts differ. According to some researchers, people came here to escape crowded coasts or invading armies. Either way, the idea stuck for a very long time.

scenes.narration: Life down here was never easy, though. I read an interview with a woman who grew up in one of these homes. She told the Associated Press she remembered carrying water by camel from a spring far away, and searching for food every day. Bigger homes had several courtyards joined by tunnels, like a family that kept adding rooms instead of moving. Similar underground homes exist across the border in Libya, but around Matmata they became a whole landscape. I tried carrying a pair of buckets of water up the tunnel ramp. I made it halfway, sat down, and drank most of the water. That is why camels were involved.

scenes.narration: I want to tell this part plainly. In a place this dry, the danger you least expect is rain. In the late nineteen sixties, severe flooding hit the region. Water poured into the pits, and many homes collapsed. According to some accounts, the area had been little known to outsiders until then, and that people sought help from the central government. At the same time, Tunisia's president Habib Bourguiba was pushing to modernise the country. In the nineteen sixties and seventies, new towns and villages were built above ground. Many families moved into them. Houses that had sheltered generations were left empty, and some slowly filled with sand.

scenes.narration: Then came the strangest twist. Start with one courtyard, belonging to one family. In nineteen sixty-nine, that traditional home became a hotel, the Hotel Sidi Driss. Zoom out: in nineteen seventy-six, a film crew arrived, and the hotel was used as a location for the very first Star Wars film. Zoom out again: for decades since, fans have come from all over the world to stand in that courtyard. Tourism now helps keep the old homes alive. Reuters met families still living underground on the outskirts of Matmata, who let tourists visit in return for tips. One woman told Reuters that leaving her house would be like throwing away her life and her traditions. I stood in the hotel courtyard among people taking photos, and I thought about her. The visitors came for a film. The house was here first.

scenes.narration: That night I slept in the hotel, in a small vaulted room off one of its courtyards. The walls were thick and white and curved, like sleeping inside a very large, very polite egg. At dinner, people at the long tables compared photos and argued about which doorway was in which scene. I ordered couscous and argued with nobody. The couscous was excellent and did not appear in any film. Around midnight I went up the ramp to look at the stars and came back down the wrong tunnel. Every courtyard looks the same in the dark if you are the kind of traveller who does not count doorways. I found my room by its door, which had my shoe propped against it. In the morning I counted the doorways properly. I had been off by a whole courtyard.

scenes.narration: So why do some people still live below ground, when a house with windows is right up the road? Part of it is comfort. The rock really does keep the heat out. Part of it is income from visitors. But mostly, from everything I read, it is home. These are houses grandparents dug, rooms where children were born, a courtyard where the whole family eats under one round piece of sky. Moving up the hill means a newer house, but not that house. I spent my last night underground, watching stars cross the circle above the courtyard, one after another, like they were being lowered in on a string.

scenes.chapter: Would I Move Into a Hole?
scenes.role: về bàn: ghép các mảnh 'vì sao', phán quyết WOULD MOVE, callback mẩu vách, câu hỏi kéo bình luận
scenes.narration: So here is the whole answer, in one piece of wall. The earth here is soft enough to dig and thick enough to keep the heat out. A pit gives you light, air and a private courtyard, and a tunnel keeps you safe. When floods and new towns pulled many families up into ordinary houses, some stayed below, because the hole in the ground was their home. Would I move there? Yes. My verdict is WOULD MOVE, as long as someone else carries the water. It suits people who love quiet, cool rooms and looking up at a round sky. It does not suit anyone who needs a view of the street, or who panics when it rains. I put the piece of wall on my desk. It is still dropping a little sand, very politely. Would you trade your windows for a courtyard full of sky?

verdict.label: WOULD MOVE
verdict.reason: A home that stays cool in the desert heat, wraps a family around its own courtyard and has kept generations sheltered is worth the dig, as long as the water problem is solved.

claims.quote: In southern Tunisia, some families live in rooms carved around a hole in the ground.
claims.statement: In southern Tunisia around Matmata, some families live in traditional homes with rooms carved around a sunken pit courtyard.

claims.quote: For centuries, Amazigh families, often called Berbers, have lived here in homes dug down into the earth.
claims.statement: For centuries, Amazigh (Berber) people in the Matmata area of southern Tunisia have lived in underground homes.

claims.quote: Matmata is about three hundred and sixty-five kilometres to the south. That's around two hundred and twenty-five miles.
claims.statement: Matmata lies about 365 km (about 225 miles) south of Tunis.

claims.quote: Then palm trees in the valleys
claims.statement: The landscape around Matmata includes palm trees and olive groves in a cratered terrain.

claims.quote: First you dig a big round pit, roughly five to ten metres across and up to about nine metres deep.
claims.statement: Matmata pit homes are built around a central courtyard pit usually 5 to 10 metres in diameter and no deeper than about 9 metres.

claims.quote: Around its walls you carve rooms into the soft rock, often on two levels. Bedrooms, the kitchen and animal stalls go on the lower level. Storage goes up top.
claims.statement: In Matmata pit homes, rooms are carved on two levels: sleeping rooms, kitchen and stables on the lower level and storage on the upper level.

claims.quote: To get in from outside, you walk down a sloping tunnel dug through the ground.
claims.statement: Matmata pit houses are entered through a sloping tunnel-like ramp from ground level.

claims.quote: One study of these homes found the inside can be up to about fifteen degrees Celsius cooler than outside in summer. That's around twenty-seven degrees Fahrenheit.
claims.statement: In summer the temperature difference between the outside and inside of Matmata cave dwellings can reach about 15 °C (about 27 °F).

claims.quote: Reuters describes these homes as having an earthen casing that protects against searing summer heat and winter winds.
claims.statement: Reuters describes Matmata's underground houses as having an earthen casing that protects against summer heat and winter winds.

claims.quote: The rock here is soft enough to dig with simple tools.
claims.statement: The Matmata pit houses are dug into soft clay-gypsum and sandstone layers.

claims.quote: From a distance, these homes are almost invisible, and the only way in is a narrow sloping tunnel, easy to watch.
claims.statement: Matmata pit houses are hard to see from a distance and can only be approached via an easily monitored tunnel-like ramp.

claims.quote: Nobody knows for certain when or why the first pits were dug, and accounts differ. According to some researchers, people came here to escape crowded coasts or invading armies.
claims.statement: The origins of Matmata's pit houses are unclear; suggested explanations include escaping overpopulated coastal regions or fleeing conquerors.

claims.quote: I read an interview with a woman who grew up in one of these homes. She told the Associated Press she remembered carrying water by camel from a spring far away, and searching for food every day.
claims.statement: A former resident of the Matmata home that became the Hotel Sidi Driss told the Associated Press she remembered carrying water by camel from a distant spring and searching daily for food.

claims.quote: Bigger homes had several courtyards joined by tunnels
claims.statement: Some larger Matmata dwellings include several courtyards connected by underground passages.

claims.quote: Similar underground homes exist across the border in Libya
claims.statement: Similar underground homes are found across the border in Libya.

claims.quote: In the late nineteen sixties, severe flooding hit the region. Water poured into the pits, and many homes collapsed. According to some accounts, the area had been little known to outsiders until then, and that people sought help from the central government.
claims.statement: Severe flooding in the late 1960s inundated Matmata's pit homes and caused many to collapse; accounts say the region was little known to outsiders until then, when locals sought aid from the central government.

claims.quote: At the same time, Tunisia's president Habib Bourguiba was pushing to modernise the country. In the nineteen sixties and seventies, new towns and villages were built above ground. Many families moved into them.
claims.statement: Many families left Tunisia's underground houses when new towns and villages were built in the 1960s and 1970s under President Habib Bourguiba's modernisation drive.

claims.quote: In nineteen sixty-nine, that traditional home became a hotel, the Hotel Sidi Driss.
claims.statement: The Hotel Sidi Driss in Matmata was a traditional Berber home before becoming a hotel in 1969.

claims.quote: Zoom out: in nineteen seventy-six, a film crew arrived, and the hotel was used as a location for the very first Star Wars film.
claims.statement: The Hotel Sidi Driss in Matmata was used in 1976 as a filming location for the first Star Wars film, A New Hope.

claims.quote: Tourism now helps keep the old homes alive. Reuters met families still living underground on the outskirts of Matmata, who let tourists visit in return for tips. One woman told Reuters that leaving her house would be like throwing away her life and her traditions.
claims.statement: Reuters reported in 2018 that a few families still live in underground houses around Matmata and let tourists visit for tips; one resident said leaving would be like throwing away her life and traditions.
